read.sections.0.text.note: "from the 1400s to the 1800s" written ตั้งแต่ช่วงปี 1400 ถึงช่วงปี 1800 (KEY_TERMS gives ช่วงปี 1400 ถึง 1499 for one century, which is clumsy in a range). Check it reads as four centuries, not exact years. Thu Bồn River written แม่น้ำทูโบน: check the usual Thai spelling. Hội An is ฮอยอัน. Second pass, one style for centuries across the course: one century is ช่วงปี 1400 ถึง 1499 (KEY_TERMS); a run of two or more is ช่วงปี 1400 ถึง 1800 กว่า ("1400 to 1800-something": accurate to the end of the last century and keeps the English numbers for the checker); late/early is ปลายช่วงปี 700 ถึง 799 / ต้นช่วงปี 900 ถึง 999; picture labels and year labels use a dash (ช่วงปี 1400–1499). Where the English itself says '15th century' (teachers' notes, picture alt) the Thai keeps คริสต์ศตวรรษที่ 15 next to the years. ช่วงปี 1400 alone (which reads as 'around 1400') and ช่วงปีคริสต์ศักราช 700 กว่า are gone. A native speaker should confirm กว่า reads well.
read.sections.0.text.source: Hội An is a town in central Viet Nam, near the place where the Thu Bồn River meets the sea. From the 1400s to the 1800s, it was a busy trading port. Boats brought goods by water, and people on land sold, loaded and carried them. The river and the sea connected the town with traders from other parts of Asia, and later from Europe. But not everyone in Hội An was a visiting trader. Local people built their lives there too. The town's location helps explain why a port grew there. It cannot tell us who had power, or how each family lived.
read.sections.0.text.back: Hội An is a town in central Vietnam, near where the Thu Bồn River flows into the sea. From the 1400s to the 1800s, Hội An was a busy trading port town. Boats brought goods by water, and people on land sold, loaded, unloaded and carried them. The river and the sea connected this town with traders from other parts of Asia, and later from Europe. But not everyone in Hội An was a visiting trader; local people built their own lives there too. The town's location helps explain why the port grew there, but cannot tell us who had power or how each family lived.

read.sections.0.simpler.source: Hội An is a town in Viet Nam. It is near a river and the sea. For about 400 years, it was a busy port. Boats came with goods. People on land sold and carried the goods. Traders came from other parts of Asia, and later from Europe. Local people lived there too. The river helps us see why a port grew here. It does not tell us how each family lived.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: Hội An is a town in Vietnam, near a river and the sea. Hội An was a busy port for about 400 years. Boats came with goods. People on land sold and carried the goods. Traders came from other parts of Asia, and later from Europe. Local people lived there too. The river helps us see why the port grew here, but does not tell how each family lived.

read.sections.1.text.source: In 1999, UNESCO, a part of the United Nations, listed Hội An as a World Heritage site. Its description says the old town has shops, homes, an open market and a ferry quay. Many buildings face the street, so customers could walk in. Their backs open to the river, so goods could go on and off boats. From this, we can make an inference: the river and the street were both important for trade. UNESCO says the buildings mix local ways with mostly Chinese and Japanese ideas, and later European ones. This is a modern account, not a diary from a trader in the 1500s.
read.sections.1.text.back: In 1999, UNESCO, part of the United Nations, listed Hội An as a World Heritage site. UNESCO's description says the old town has shops, houses, an open-air market and ferry quays. Many buildings face the street, so customers could walk in. The back opens onto the river, so goods could be loaded onto and off boats. From this, we can make an inference: both the river and the street mattered for trade. UNESCO says the buildings mix local styles with ideas mostly from China and Japan, and later from Europe. This is a modern account, not the diary of a trader in the 1500s.

read.sections.2.text.source: The second picture is a photo of a covered bridge in Hội An, taken in 2018. The bridge is part of the town's heritage, a place people value and look after today. The photo shows what the bridge looked like on that day. It cannot show the first traders who used the port centuries ago, or what every resident thought. The map helps us see possible connections, and the photo lets us look at a place now. To hear a resident's view from long ago, we would need other sources, such as old records or objects.
read.sections.2.text.back: The second picture is a photo of the covered bridge in Hội An, taken in 2018. This bridge is part of the town's heritage, a place people value and look after today. A map helps us see possible connections, and a photo helps us look at the place now. To hear the views of past residents, we need other sources, such as old records or objects.

watch.summary.source: This is a short film of a few minutes. NHK, a broadcaster from Japan, made it with UNESCO. It is part of a series of films about World Heritage sites. UNESCO's record of the film says it is about the old town and its covered bridge, often called the Japanese Bridge. The record describes Hội An in a few words. Hội An is an old trading port that has been well looked after. It was a port from the 1400s to the 1800s. Its buildings and its street plan show a mix of local ways and ideas from other places. Remember that a camera films a place on one day. The film shows Hội An in modern times, not the busy port of long ago.
watch.summary.back: This is a short film a few minutes long. NHK, a television station from Japan, made it with UNESCO as part of a series about World Heritage sites. UNESCO's record about this film says it is about the old town and the covered bridge, often called the Japanese Bridge. That record describes Hội An briefly: Hội An is a well-preserved old trading port town. It was a port from the 1400s to the 1800s. The town's buildings and street layout show a mix of local styles and ideas from elsewhere. Remember the camera filmed the place on one day. This film shows Hội An in modern times, not the busy port of the past.

educatorNotes.1.note: "with a pagoda on it" written ที่มีศาลเจ้าอยู่บนสะพาน (the Japanese Bridge's small temple); check the word. "18th century" is คริสต์ศตวรรษที่ 18.
educatorNotes.1.source: Misconception to address: that a later photo is a picture of the port's earlier daily life. Also, "Chinese and Japanese influences" in buildings do not tell us every resident's ancestry, and local people were not passive; the bridge's popular name does not tell us who built or used it. UNESCO's listing dates the wooden bridge, with a pagoda on it, to the 18th century, while other accounts give an earlier first bridge, so the lesson does not date it. Source caveats: UNESCO's account is a modern interpretation of surviving buildings; the photo shows a lower modern footbridge in front and crowds of visitors in 2018. For an optional comparison with another port that records local voices, see George Town World Heritage Incorporated's oral history work, but do not make it a second case.
educatorNotes.1.back: Misconceptions to address: that a later photo is a picture of daily life in the old port. Also, "Chinese and Japanese influence" in the buildings doesn't tell us every resident's ancestry, and local people were not only on the receiving end. The bridge's popular name doesn't say who built or used it. UNESCO's listing says the wooden bridge with a shrine on it was built in the 18th century (1700–1799), but other accounts say there was an older first bridge, so the lesson gives no date for the bridge. Source caution: UNESCO's account is a modern interpretation of the buildings that remain. The photo shows a lower modern wooden walkway bridge in front and many tourists in 2018. To compare with another port that recorded local voices, see George Town World Heritage Incorporated's oral history work, but don't make it a second case study.
